name: Palm Beach Reef
coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid (approx. 19th Avenue, Palm Beach); x = alongshore (positive toward north, the predominant sand-transport / downdrift direction per the City of Gold Coast's own explainer video [S1]); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0

crest_depth_m.datum: below mean sea level at the reef's highest point (≈0.6 m below lowest astronomical tide)

distance_offshore_m.measured_from: shoreline near 19th Avenue, Palm Beach (exact measurement point — near edge, far edge, or centroid — not specified by any source; we placed the polygon centroid at y=270 as a simplifying assumption, see derivation/open_issues)

orientation_notes: Elongated, rounded, asymmetric rock mound. Read off the two available plan-view graphics (the labelled aerial/schematic diagrams on Cru Collective's site, sourced from the project team) and cross-checked against the visible rock-shadow patch in the ABC News aerial photo, the mound tapers to a narrower, rounded point on its shoreward (near-shore) side and broadens to a blunter, rounded mass on its seaward (offshore) side — the opposite taper direction from Gemini's assumed 'apex seaward' chevron (see gemini_comparison). Long axis (160 m) treated as alongshore, short axis (80 m) as cross-shore, matching the conventional reading of '160 m long × 80 m wide' in every source, though no source explicitly labels which figure is alongshore vs cross-shore (flagged in open_issues). The reef sits in the lee of Palm Beach's natural offshore reef [R3], targeting dominant east-to-southeast swell [R2][R15], with sand naturally transported north along this stretch of coast [S1] — hence x-positive is defined as north. No source gives a numeric shoreline bearing or swell-approach angle; Gemini's '345° NNW shoreline / 090–110° swell' figures are not supported by any source we found and are not reproduced here.
materials: Quarried rock boulders, up to 8 t each (max individual weight, stated directly by S1, R4, R7, R16; re-verified 2026-09-25) — R2 separately describes a design-evolution note, "The rock size was increased from 3 tons to 5 and 8 ton rocks," implying discrete size classes rather than a continuous range; no source states a minimum boulder weight or a formal "X–8 t" range. [Verification 2026-09-25: an earlier draft of this file stated "4–8 t each" and attributed the range to R16; R16 was re-fetched and found to state only "up to eight tonne," with no minimum — the "4 t" figure was unsupported and has been removed.] Total ~60,000 tonnes [R7, R9 — both state "60,000 tonnes" directly; R2/R4/R16 do not give a total-tonnage figure], ~25,000 m³ by volume [R13]; rock type (e.g. basalt/granite) is not specified in any source we found [R2][R4][R7][R9][R13][R16]

open_issues: Width (80 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 144 m) and distance offshore (270 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 330 m) remain unresolved across every source checked, including this one — carried forward unchanged from the card [R5].

No source explicitly states which published figure (160 m or 80 m) is the alongshore dimension vs the cross-shore dimension; we assumed 160 m = alongshore and 80 m = cross-shore, matching the conventional reading and Gemini's own assumption, but this is an inference, not a stated fact.

The point from which '270 m offshore' is measured (near edge, far edge, or centroid) is not specified by any source; we assumed centroid for simplicity, which shifts the true near/far edges by roughly ±40-45 m depending on which convention the original designers used.

Verification 2026-09-25 flags an internal tension: our own reading of the Cru Collective schematic (images_relied_on #1) concludes the '270m' arrow visually lands on the reef's near/shoreward edge, not its centroid — yet the polygon below places the centroid (not the near edge) at y=270. If the near-edge reading is right, the whole polygon should sit roughly 40m further offshore than drawn (shoreward tip near y=266 instead of y=226, centroid near y=310 instead of y=270). This was not corrected in the polygon itself (doing so would require a new speculative construction, which this adversarial-check task's scope does not extend to), but is flagged here as an unresolved self-consistency issue for a future revision.

No true as-built CAD drawing or bathymetric survey of the constructed reef was found publicly (despite Gemini's citation, which does not correspond to any real accessible document); our polygon's exact vertex geometry is a qualitative estimate from a non-scaled marketing schematic plus a real aerial photo, not a measurement, and should be treated as illustrative of shape family (elongated, rounded, shoreward-tapered mound) rather than a precise outline.
Precise lat/lon of the reef structure itself (as opposed to the 19th Avenue onshore reference point) was not found in any source.
Net footprint area (~9,678 m2 here) is a geometric consequence of our assumed polygon shape, not an independently published or measured figure; treat as low-confidence.

verification.item: Plan-view shape / taper direction (narrow shoreward, broad seaward)
verification.evidence: Downloaded and directly viewed all three cited images (Completion2.jpg, Completion.jpg, ABC aerial) at high zoom. Completion2.jpg does show a shape narrower/pointed at the arrow (shoreward) end and blunter/wider at the far (seaward) end, consistent with the card's claim, and the '270m' arrow visually lands on the icon's near tip, not its center -- but the icon itself is a generic stock-style 3D rock graphic, not a purpose-drawn technical plan, so this is weak evidence. Completion.jpg's icon is too small/low-res to independently confirm taper direction. The ABC aerial photo's dark patch is elongated and roughly consistent with the claimed taper, but the active dredger sits at the patch's near/broad end, so dredging turbidity may be inflating that end's apparent width -- a confound not previously flagged. Net: the taper-direction call remains the best-supported reading available (better than Gemini's citation-free opposite claim) but should be read as plausible, weakly-evidenced qualitative shape family, not a confirmed geometric fact -- consistent with (and now more explicitly caveated than) the card's existing 'High uncertainty' label.
